newsitem.title: PANAMA: Panama phone co sale promises long-awaited revamp.
newsitem.headline: Panama phone co sale promises long-awaited revamp.

text.p: Crossed lines, wearying waits for new phones, and appalling service should be history after Panama's May 20 sale of a portion of state telephone company INTEL.

"The important thing is the quality of phone service getting better. It now takes from three days to a maximum of eight years to get a telephone," said Rigoberto Munoz Diaz, INTEL executive vice president of development.

Telecommunications giants GTE Corp of the United States and Britain's Cable and Wireless Plc are the only companies that have qualified to participate in the sale of 49 percent of the National Telecommunications Institute (INTEL).
Although INTEL is said to be worth some $2 billion, government officials have not given estimates of its value.
"This is (Panama's) largest privatization ever in terms of dollar amount," noted Alfredo Macia, head of the country's privatization effort.
But the government admits better service is long overdue in Panama.

The contract calls for making the system 100 percent digital, improving service and response time, and installing more public telephones over five years. Domestic and long-distance rates are expected to drop. The winner will receive a concession to manage INTEL for 20 years.
Munoz said the contract also stipulated that the company must have Band B cellular service -- one of two cellular bands -- in operation within 12 months.
Last year, a consortium led by BellSouth Corp won the license to build and operate Panama's first cellular telephone network, Band A, with a bid of $72.61 million.
The government estimates that the winner will invest at least $500 million over five years in upgrades, and increase the number of telephone lines to 800,000 from 330,000.
"That's not in the concession contract, but (those are) government estimates on the number of lines we'll need and how much the company would need to spend," Munoz said.
The company will be obliged under the contract to ensure new phones are installed within three days for a minimum of 95 percent of customers requesting a line.
"We have certain requirements to improve and maintain the quality of service. If the economy is going well, we will go from 12.2 phones per 100 inhabitants to 25 phones per 100," he said.
The number of coin- and card-operated public telephones is expected to increase from 1.17 per 1,000 inhabitants to nearly 4 under the contract.
"Public telephone service is very bad now. It will improve, especially for poor people who will be able to buy a (phone) card from $5 to $24," Munoz said.
Panama banned state-owned companies from participating in the sale, shutting out many European and Asian firms.

"We wanted to avoid a government-run company to be operated by a foreign government company. It came as a relief to everyone when Cable & Wireless entered," Macia explained. For a while, only GTE had entered the running for INTEL.
He said Panama's telecommunications future looked bright.
"Since Panama is such a small market, either company (GTE or C&W) will bring a tremendous advantage."
((-- Panama City newsroom, 507 2237739))
